policy.statement: Every applicable EF Core relational specification behavior must run. A skip is permitted only for a primary-source-backed database-engine limitation, an upstream EF Core limitation reached before provider-owned translation can solve it, or a structurally inapplicable historical test.
engineLimitationRequirements: At least one official database-vendor primary source
A retrieval date for every source
A reproducible probe against every affected supported target
frameworkLimitationRequirements: The upstream EF Core specification test is itself skipped and is backed by either its linked dotnet/efcore issue or both the exact upstream skip source and the framework enforcement source
The failure is reproduced with the upstream skip disabled
The failure is attributable to framework-owned translation or semantics rather than provider SQL capability
A retrieval date and concrete re-evaluation trigger

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 stored functions return one scalar value and cannot expose a parameterized relational rowset in a FROM clause.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Stored Routine Syntax
primarySources.supports: The manual defines a stored function as callable inside an expression and states that it returns a scalar value; it defines procedures, rather than functions, as the routine form that can return result sets.

primarySources.title: Stored Function Overview
primarySources.supports: The overview defines a stored function as a routine invoked in an SQL statement that returns one value.

primarySources.title: CREATE FUNCTION
primarySources.supports: The complete grammar requires RETURNS followed by a MariaDB data type, and its SELECT-body documentation requires the subquery to return one scalar value.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: Stored Routine Syntax
primarySources.supports: The manual defines stored functions as statement expressions that return a scalar value; procedures are the routine form that can return result sets.

observations.result: All 26 rowset-function invocations fail at execution because the generated FROM function-name(arguments) shape is not part of MySQL grammar; the 80 scalar and non-rowset UDF contracts pass after fixture seeding.
All 26 rowset-function invocations fail at execution because the generated FROM function-name(arguments) shape is not part of MySQL 9.7 grammar; scalar and non-rowset UDF contracts pass.
All 26 rowset-function invocations fail at the FROM function-name(arguments) syntax boundary; scalar stored functions remain executable on MariaDB 10.11.
All 26 rowset-function invocations fail at the same FROM function-name(arguments) syntax boundary; scalar stored functions remain executable.
All 26 rowset-function invocations fail at the same FROM function-name(arguments) syntax boundary; MariaDB 11.8 has not added a table-valued stored-function form.
All 26 rowset-function invocations fail at the FROM function-name(arguments) syntax boundary; MariaDB 12.3 has not added a table-valued stored-function form.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: A view cannot accept the correlated parameters required by these contracts. A stored procedure can return a result set but cannot participate as a composable table source in SELECT, JOIN, APPLY, filtering, grouping, or nested subqueries. Replacing the operation with client evaluation would change server-side query semantics and execution cardinality. JSON_TABLE accepts JSON documents rather than an arbitrary parameterized relational routine and therefore cannot preserve the general table-valued-function contract.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when a supported MySQL or MariaDB release documents a parameterized table-valued stored function or another composable routine form that can be referenced from FROM and joined like a relational table.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 native TIME values retain at most six fractional-second digits, while System.TimeSpan retains seven decimal digits at 100-nanosecond resolution.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Fractional Seconds in Time Values
primarySources.supports: The manual limits TIME, DATETIME, and TIMESTAMP fractional-second precision to microseconds, with an fsp range from 0 through 6.

primarySources.title: Microseconds in MariaDB
primarySources.supports: The documentation states that TIME, DATETIME, and TIMESTAMP precision is the number of fractional digits and can range only from 0 through 6.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: Fractional Seconds in Time Values
primarySources.supports: The manual limits TIME, DATETIME, and TIMESTAMP fractional-second precision to an fsp range from 0 through 6.

observations.result: The native datetime(7) and time(7) mapping probes fail because MySQL accepts only precisions 0 through 6. All six sync and async TPH, TPT, and TPC invocations materialize 02:00:15.4562010 instead of the source TimeSpan value 02:00:15.4562014 because TIME(6) cannot retain the seventh fractional digit.
The native datetime(7) and time(7) mapping probes fail because MySQL 9.7 accepts only precisions 0 through 6. All six query invocations lose the seventh TimeSpan fractional digit.
The native datetime(7) and time(7) mapping probes fail because MariaDB 10.11 accepts only precisions 0 through 6. All six query invocations lose the seventh TimeSpan digit.

The native datetime(7) and time(7) mapping probes fail because MariaDB accepts only precisions 0 through 6. All six query invocations lose the seventh TimeSpan fractional digit at the same native TIME(6) storage boundary.

The native datetime(7) and time(7) mapping probes fail because MariaDB accepts only precisions 0 through 6. All six query invocations lose the seventh TimeSpan fractional digit; MariaDB 11.8 retains the same documented microsecond ceiling.
The native datetime(7) and time(7) mapping probes fail because MariaDB 12.3 accepts only precisions 0 through 6. All six query invocations lose the seventh TimeSpan digit.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Changing the provider-wide TimeSpan mapping to text or integer ticks would alter existing schemas, native TIME ordering and functions, interoperability, and migration semantics. Client evaluation would also change query execution. Applications that require exact 100-nanosecond persistence can opt into a value converter and a non-temporal store type, but the provider cannot transparently preserve the missing digit in a native TIME column.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probes when a supported MySQL or MariaDB release documents native temporal precision beyond six fractional-second digits, or when EF Core introduces a distinct exact-duration mapping contract that does not require the native TIME type.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 reject syntactically invalid JSON documents before EF Core can exercise its malformed-document materialization contract.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: The JSON Data Type
primarySources.supports: The manual states that values stored in native JSON columns are validated and that invalid documents produce an error.

primarySources.title: JSON Data Type
primarySources.supports: MariaDB documents JSON as a LONGTEXT alias with an automatically included JSON_VALID constraint that guarantees valid JSON documents.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: The JSON Data Type
primarySources.supports: The manual states that native JSON values are validated and invalid documents produce an error.

observations.result: All four tracking and no-tracking cases reach the exact upstream malformed-document seed and fail with MySQL invalid-JSON errors before query materialization.
Both malformed-document methods fail for synchronous and asynchronous rows because MySQL 9.7 validates native JSON before the EF Core materializer can read the document.
Both malformed-document methods fail for synchronous and asynchronous rows because MariaDB 10.11 enforces JSON_VALID before the EF Core materializer reads the document.
All four cases reach the exact upstream malformed-document seed and fail its JSON_VALID constraint before query materialization.
All four cases reach the exact upstream malformed-document seed and fail its JSON_VALID constraint before query materialization.
Both malformed-document methods fail for synchronous and asynchronous rows because MariaDB 12.3 enforces JSON_VALID before the EF Core materializer reads the document.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Mapping the properties to unvalidated text would change the relational schema, native JSON validation, JSON function semantics, and reverse-engineering contract. Rewriting malformed documents into valid JSON would alter the values that the tests intentionally require EF Core to materialize. The provider cannot make the engines accept invalid native JSON without changing the tested behavior.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when a supported MySQL or MariaDB release documents a native JSON storage mode that can retain syntactically invalid documents, or when EF Core replaces the malformed-document contract with one that uses a text store type.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 reject POINT EMPTY input instead of storing the empty point required by the inherited spatial round-trip contract.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Argument Handling
primarySources.supports: The manual states that an empty geometry is geometrically undefined and that the only valid empty geometry representation is an empty geometry collection.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Argument Handling
primarySources.supports: The manual defines invalid GIS input handling; the executable probe confirms POINT EMPTY is rejected on MySQL 9.7.

observations.result: The Point.Empty case reaches ST_GeomFromText('POINT EMPTY') and MySQL rejects it as invalid GIS data; the remaining static spatial-member cases execute.
The Point.Empty case reaches ST_GeomFromText('POINT EMPTY') and MySQL 9.7 rejects it as invalid GIS data; the remaining static spatial-member cases execute.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Rewriting Point.Empty to GeometryCollection.Empty would change the geometry subtype, CLR materialization result, and SQL type semantics. A sentinel point would no longer be empty. MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 execute the same official test, so the disposition is intentionally limited to MySQL 8.4/9.7.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when a supported MySQL release documents and accepts an empty Point representation as distinct from an empty GeometryCollection.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 native geometry storage is two-dimensional and does not preserve NetTopologySuite Z or M ordinates.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: The Geometry Class Hierarchy
primarySources.supports: The manual defines Point as a single location in coordinate space represented by its X and Y coordinates.

primarySources.title: Information Schema GEOMETRY_COLUMNS Table
primarySources.supports: MariaDB documents the geometry coordinate dimension as 2 for geometry columns.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: The Geometry Class Hierarchy
primarySources.supports: The geometry model defines Point by X and Y coordinates and does not define native Z or M ordinates.

observations.result: Round-tripping Point Z, Point M, and Point ZM through native POINT columns returns NaN for the additional ordinates instead of the source values.
Round-tripping through MySQL 9.7 native POINT columns returns NaN for Z and M instead of preserving the source ordinates.
Round-tripping through MariaDB 10.11 native POINT columns returns NaN for Z and M at the documented two-dimensional storage boundary.
Round-tripping through native POINT columns returns NaN for the Z and M ordinates at the same two-dimensional storage boundary.
Round-tripping through native POINT columns returns NaN for the Z and M ordinates; MariaDB 11.8 retains the documented two-dimensional geometry model.
Round-tripping through MariaDB 12.3 native POINT columns returns NaN for Z and M; the native geometry model remains two-dimensional.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Sidecar columns or custom binary serialization could retain Z and M, but would change the model schema, native geometry representation, spatial indexes and functions, reverse engineering, and interoperability. The provider cannot transparently add ordinates to a native two-dimensional POINT column.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when a supported MySQL or MariaDB release documents native Z, M, or ZM geometry dimensions and preserves those ordinates through spatial storage and retrieval.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 expose no server function that implements NetTopologySuite geometry normalization.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Reference
primarySources.supports: The exhaustive MySQL 8.4 spatial function inventory contains no geometry normalization, geometry reversal, or ST_Relate function.

primarySources.title: Geometry Statements
primarySources.supports: The exhaustive MariaDB geometry statement inventory contains no geometry normalization or geometry reversal function.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Reference
primarySources.supports: The complete spatial function inventory contains no geometry normalization operation.

observations.result: Both synchronous and asynchronous invocations fail because the engine has no normalization function and the expression therefore reaches client evaluation over server-null rows.
Both invocations fail because MySQL 9.7 has no normalization function and the expression therefore reaches client evaluation over server-null rows.
Both invocations fail at the missing server-side geometry-normalization boundary on MariaDB 10.11.
Both invocations fail at the same missing server-operation boundary as MySQL 8.4.
Both invocations fail at the same missing server-operation boundary as MariaDB 11.4.
Both invocations fail at the missing server-side geometry-normalization boundary on MariaDB 12.3.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Normalization is defined over arbitrary geometry types, nested collections, ring orientation, and component ordering. The available scalar spatial functions neither expose a generic geometry tree nor provide the canonical comparison and reconstruction primitive required to express that algorithm as a composable SQL expression. Client normalization would change server-side projection semantics and null handling, while installing a stored routine is outside a provider's deployment authority.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when every supported engine documents a server-side geometry normalization function or a composable equivalent over arbitrary geometry values.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 expose no server function for evaluating an arbitrary DE-9IM relation pattern.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Reference
primarySources.supports: The exhaustive MySQL 8.4 spatial function inventory contains no geometry normalization, geometry reversal, or ST_Relate function.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Reference
primarySources.supports: The complete spatial function inventory contains no arbitrary DE-9IM relation-pattern function.

observations.result: Both synchronous and asynchronous invocations fail because MySQL 8.4 has no server translation for an arbitrary DE-9IM relation pattern.
Both synchronous and asynchronous invocations fail because MySQL 9.7 has no server translation for an arbitrary DE-9IM relation pattern.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Individual named topological predicates cover only fixed DE-9IM masks. They cannot preserve the general Relate contract, which accepts arbitrary nine-intersection patterns, and client evaluation would change server-side query semantics.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when MySQL documents ST_Relate or another server-side operation accepting an arbitrary DE-9IM matrix pattern.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 expose no server function that reverses arbitrary geometry coordinate order.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Reference
primarySources.supports: The exhaustive MySQL 8.4 spatial function inventory contains no geometry normalization, geometry reversal, or ST_Relate function.

primarySources.title: Geometry Statements
primarySources.supports: The exhaustive MariaDB geometry statement inventory contains no geometry normalization or geometry reversal function.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: Spatial Function Reference
primarySources.supports: The complete spatial function inventory contains no arbitrary geometry reversal operation.

observations.result: Both synchronous and asynchronous invocations fail because the engine has no geometry reversal function and the expression reaches client evaluation over server-null rows.
Both invocations fail because MySQL 9.7 has no geometry reversal function and the expression reaches client evaluation over server-null rows.
Both invocations fail at the missing server-side geometry-reversal boundary on MariaDB 10.11.
Both invocations fail at the same missing server-operation boundary as MySQL 8.4.
Both invocations fail at the same missing server-operation boundary as MariaDB 11.4.
Both invocations fail at the missing server-side geometry-reversal boundary on MariaDB 12.3.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: The operation must reverse coordinate and component order recursively while preserving each arbitrary runtime geometry subtype. The engines expose neither a generic geometry-tree iterator nor a generic reconstruction expression, so named point, line, polygon, and collection functions cannot form one semantics-preserving composable translation. Client reversal is not an equivalent server query.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when every supported engine documents a server-side reverse function for arbitrary geometry values.

activeDispositions.summary: MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 ST_Buffer does not accept the strategy argument required by the inherited buffer-with-configuration contract.

primarySources.title: ST_BUFFER
primarySources.supports: The documented MariaDB syntax is ST_BUFFER(g1, r); it exposes no strategy or quadrant-segment argument.

observations.result: Both invocations fail with an incorrect parameter-count error when the required buffer strategy is supplied to MariaDB 10.11 ST_Buffer.
Both synchronous and asynchronous invocations fail with an incorrect parameter-count error when the required buffer strategy is supplied.
Both invocations fail with the same two-argument ST_Buffer boundary as MariaDB 11.4.
Both invocations fail with an incorrect parameter-count error when the required buffer strategy is supplied to MariaDB 12.3 ST_Buffer.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Dropping the quadrant-segment value changes buffer approximation and therefore results. No other MariaDB 11.x spatial function accepts this strategy or can post-process a two-argument buffer into the requested approximation.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when MariaDB documents ST_Buffer strategy arguments or a semantics-equivalent quadrant-segment operation on every supported MariaDB target.

activeDispositions.summary: MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8 do not provide ST_Collect; the function is available from MariaDB 12.0 and the MariaDB 12.3 target executes these contracts.

primarySources.title: ST_Collect
primarySources.supports: The official reference marks ST_Collect as available from MariaDB 12.0; neither supported MariaDB 11.x target provides it.

primarySources.title: MariaDB 12.0 Changes and Improvements
primarySources.supports: The official MariaDB 12.0 feature inventory lists ST_Collect and ST_IsValid as newly added GIS functions.

observations.result: All six synchronous and asynchronous aggregate invocations fail because ST_Collect is absent from MariaDB 10.11.
All six synchronous and asynchronous aggregate invocations fail because ST_Collect is absent.
All six invocations fail at the same missing ST_Collect boundary as MariaDB 11.4.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: The operations require one server-side geometry value aggregated from an unbounded relational group. Scalar geometry constructors cannot consume a rowset, and client aggregation would change query execution and grouping semantics.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when every supported MariaDB target provides ST_Collect or an equivalent composable spatial aggregate.

activeDispositions.summary: MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8 do not provide ST_IsValid; the function was added in MariaDB 12.0 and the MariaDB 12.3 target executes this contract.

primarySources.title: ST_IsValid
primarySources.supports: The official reference marks ST_IsValid as available from MariaDB 12.0; neither supported MariaDB 11.x target provides it.

primarySources.title: MariaDB 12.0 Changes and Improvements
primarySources.supports: The official MariaDB 12.0 feature inventory lists ST_Collect and ST_IsValid as newly added GIS functions.

observations.result: Both synchronous and asynchronous invocations fail because ST_IsValid is absent from MariaDB 10.11.
Both synchronous and asynchronous invocations fail because ST_IsValid is absent.
Both invocations fail at the same missing ST_IsValid boundary as MariaDB 11.4.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Validity checking requires the engine's topology implementation over arbitrary geometry types. The MariaDB 11.x scalar surface exposes no equivalent predicate, and reconstructing that topology algorithm as a composable provider expression is not possible.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when every supported MariaDB target provides ST_IsValid or an equivalent server-side validity predicate.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4 reject the selected self-referencing delete when the foreign-key constraint is checked immediately; MariaDB 11.8/12.3 execute it.

primarySources.title: FOREIGN KEY Constraints
primarySources.supports: The Referential Actions section states that InnoDB treats NO ACTION as RESTRICT and immediately rejects a parent delete while a related foreign-key value exists. The same page explicitly permits self-referential foreign keys.

primarySources.title: Foreign Keys
primarySources.supports: The Constraints section states that RESTRICT is the default ON DELETE behavior, NO ACTION is its synonym, and the change fails with error 1451 when a child row exists.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: FOREIGN KEY Constraints
primarySources.supports: The manual documents immediate foreign-key constraint checking and rejection of statements that violate a referencing constraint.

observations.result: Both sync and async invocations fail with error 1451 because Animals.EagleId still references the selected principal row when InnoDB checks the delete.
Both invocations fail with error 1451 because Animals.EagleId still references the selected principal row when MySQL 9.7 checks the delete.
Both invocations fail with error 1451 because Animals.EagleId still references the selected principal row when MariaDB 10.11 checks the delete.
Both sync and async invocations fail with the same error 1451 and self-referencing Animals.EagleId constraint.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: The provider already isolates the target-table subquery, so the statement reaches execution. Nulling or deleting dependent rows first would require extra DML, would change the configured NO ACTION relationship semantics when a dependent is outside the query result, and would change ExecuteDelete's affected-row contract. Disabling foreign_key_checks would weaken integrity for the whole session. No general single-statement rewrite can preserve the query, relationship, and row-count semantics under immediate RESTRICT enforcement.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when MySQL or MariaDB documents statement-end NO ACTION checks for InnoDB, or when a supported target replaces MariaDB 11.4. MariaDB 11.8 remains active because this exact specification case passes there.

activeDispositions.summary: MySQL 8.4/9.7 and MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 CREATE INDEX grammar has no WHERE predicate for filtered or partial indexes.

primarySources.title: MySQL 8.4 Reference Manual: CREATE INDEX Statement
primarySources.supports: The complete CREATE INDEX grammar permits column, prefix, or functional key parts followed by index, algorithm, and lock options; it defines no WHERE predicate or partial-index clause.

primarySources.title: CREATE INDEX
primarySources.supports: The complete CREATE INDEX grammar for the supported MariaDB lines permits column key parts and documented index options but defines no WHERE predicate or partial-index clause.

primarySources.title: MySQL 9.7 Reference Manual: CREATE INDEX Statement
primarySources.supports: The complete CREATE INDEX grammar has no WHERE predicate for filtered or partial indexes.

observations.result: Both the non-unique and unique CREATE INDEX statements fail with a syntax error at their WHERE predicate.
Both non-unique and unique CREATE INDEX statements fail with a MySQL 9.7 syntax error at the WHERE predicate.
Both CREATE INDEX statements fail with a MariaDB 10.11 syntax error at the WHERE predicate.
Both statements fail with the MariaDB syntax error at WHERE; the unique case includes the compound Name predicate.
Both statements fail with the same syntax error at WHERE, confirming that MariaDB 11.8 has not added filtered-index grammar.
Both CREATE INDEX statements fail with a MariaDB 12.3 syntax error at the WHERE predicate.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: Ignoring the predicate would silently change index storage and, for unique indexes, constraint semantics. MySQL functional key parts and generated columns can emulate only predicates accepted by generated-expression restrictions; MariaDB requires a different generated-column shape. Both approaches add synthetic schema state, change the index column identity, and cannot preserve the general relational filter contract for arbitrary predicates. There is no general semantics-preserving provider rewrite across all supported targets.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when a supported MySQL or MariaDB release adds a native predicate clause for CREATE INDEX or another native index form that preserves arbitrary relational filter semantics and reverse-engineered index identity.

primarySources.title: Issue 28525: Bulk Delete on result of First family in projection
primarySources.supports: The open backlog issue contains the same official specification shape and states that EF Core's entity projection shaper and delete structure cannot currently represent it.

observations.result: All 12 sync and async invocations fail before provider SQL generation with ExecuteDeleteOnNonEntityType.
The MySQL 9.7.2 targeted probe reproduces the existing result: All 12 sync and async invocations fail before provider SQL generation with ExecuteDeleteOnNonEntityType.
The MariaDB 10.11.18 targeted probe reproduces the existing result: All 12 sync and async invocations fail before provider SQL generation with ExecuteDeleteOnNonEntityType.

All 12 invocations fail at the same EF Core non-entity-projection boundary before provider SQL generation.
The MariaDB 12.3.2 targeted probe reproduces the existing result: All 12 sync and async invocations fail before provider SQL generation with ExecuteDeleteOnNonEntityType.

activeDispositions.frameworkBoundaryAssessment: RelationalQueryableMethodTranslatingExpressionVisitor.TranslateExecuteDelete rejects the shaped query before IsValidSelectExpressionForExecuteDelete or the provider SQL generator is invoked. A provider cannot recover the discarded entity projection through SQL translation hooks.

primarySources.supports: The official EF Core 10.0.8 specification marks Update_where_hierarchy_subquery skipped before provider subclasses run it.

primarySources.title: Relational ExecuteUpdate translation
primarySources.supports: TranslateExecuteUpdate rejects TpcTablesExpression before calling the provider-overridable IsValidSelectExpressionForExecuteUpdate method.

observations.result: Both TPC fixture variants fail in sync and async mode with ExecuteOperationOnTPC before provider update validation.
The MySQL 9.7.2 targeted probe reproduces the existing result: Both TPC fixture variants fail in sync and async mode with ExecuteOperationOnTPC before provider update validation.
The MariaDB 10.11.18 targeted probe reproduces the existing result: Both TPC fixture variants fail in sync and async mode with ExecuteOperationOnTPC before provider update validation.
Both TPC fixture variants fail at the same EF Core TpcTablesExpression guard before provider update validation.
Both TPC fixture variants fail at the same EF Core TpcTablesExpression guard before provider update validation.

activeDispositions.summary: MariaDB 10.11/11.4/11.8/12.3 cannot express a correlated derived table because FROM-subqueries cannot be correlated and the JOIN grammar has no LATERAL derived-table form.

primarySources.title: Subquery Limitations
primarySources.supports: The Correlated Subqueries section states that subqueries in the FROM clause cannot be correlated.

primarySources.title: JOIN Syntax
primarySources.supports: The complete table_reference and join_table grammar for MariaDB 11.4 through 11.8 has no LATERAL production.

observations.result: All 689 affected invocations fail at the correlated FROM-subquery or missing LATERAL boundary on MariaDB 10.11.

All 689 affected invocations fail at the correlated FROM-subquery boundary: 160 previously classified invocations plus 529 newly unmasked invocations across official query and association contracts. Representative failures are ERROR 1054 for an outer column below a derived-table boundary and the provider's explicit correlated-derived-table capability exception.
The same 689 invocations fail at the correlated FROM-subquery or missing LATERAL boundary as MariaDB 11.4.
All 689 affected invocations fail at the correlated FROM-subquery or missing LATERAL boundary on MariaDB 12.3.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: The provider flattens APPLY into ordinary joins when cardinality, null extension, ordering, and pagination semantics can be preserved; JSON_TABLE also references preceding tables directly where the relational tree permits it. The remaining tests require per-outer-row composition after DISTINCT, grouping, ordering, filtering, pagination, set operations, or nested collection shaping. That composition introduces a correlated derived-table boundary which cannot be flattened without changing results. MariaDB provides neither correlation in FROM nor an equivalent LATERAL join operator, so the general relational operation cannot be emitted as server-side SQL. Client evaluation would change the specification contract and is not accepted as a provider workaround.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when MariaDB documents either correlated FROM-subqueries or a LATERAL/APPLY join production for every supported MariaDB target.

activeDispositions.summary: MariaDB 11.4/11.8 JSON_TABLE cannot extract a JSON object or array into a JSON-typed result column; the verified 10.11 and 12.3 targets execute these contracts.

primarySources.title: JSON_TABLE
primarySources.supports: The Extracting a Subdocument into a Column section states that JSON_TABLE does not allow extraction of a JSON subdocument into a JSON column.

observations.result: Both methods fail for sync and async data rows because the required owned JSON subdocument is returned as NULL; the materializer reports Nullable object must have a value.
Both methods fail for sync and async data rows with the same NULL subdocument materialization failure as MariaDB 11.4.

activeDispositions.providerWorkaroundAssessment: The projection requires the complete owned JSON subdocument as a value so EF Core can materialize the owned graph. Extracting individual scalar members would not preserve arbitrary nested content or the specification's JSON materialization semantics. MariaDB's documented JSON_TABLE result-column restriction therefore removes the required server-side rowset operation.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when MariaDB documents JSON_TABLE support for extracting a JSON subdocument into a JSON result column on every supported MariaDB target.

primarySources.supports: The open EF Core backlog issue contains this exact specification query and explains that EF Core lacks sufficient identifier information for the projected JSON collection.

activeDispositions.frameworkBoundaryAssessment: MySqlModelValidator delegates to EF Core RelationalModelValidator, which reaches the core ModelValidator rejection before any relational command tree or provider SQL can exist. Bypassing that validation in the provider would create metadata semantics that EF Core itself does not support.
activeDispositions.reevaluateWhen: Re-run the probe when issue 35613 closes, when the consumed EF Core patch removes any linked upstream skip, or when ModelValidator no longer rejects shadow properties on complex types.
